title: Amendment & Basic Structure
summary: How the Constitution is amended, the major amendments, and the basic structure doctrine.

subcards.title: Amendment procedure (Art 368)
subcards.summary: How Parliament amends the Constitution, step by step, under Article 368.
at_a_glance: Only by a bill in either House of Parliament, brought by a minister or a private member
Special majority in each House, separately
States approve (ratify) only changes to federal provisions; at least half the States must approve, each by a simple majority
Cannot destroy the basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati case (1973))

items: Article 368 is in Part XX of the Constitution. Its title: 'Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor'.
Under Article 368(1), Parliament uses its 'constituent power' (the power to change the Constitution itself, not just make ordinary laws).
Parliament can amend any provision 'by way of addition, variation or repeal' (add new text, change text, or remove text).
So the amending power is given to Parliament by the Constitution itself. The Constitution also limits that power.
Limit: Parliament cannot change the 'basic structure' (the core features) of the Constitution — Kesavananda Bharati case (1973).
The Preamble can also be amended under Article 368, but again without touching the basic structure (it was amended once, by the 42nd Amendment, 1976).
Source: the amendment procedure (and the election of Rajya Sabha members) was borrowed from the Constitution of South Africa.
Laxmikanth: India's procedure is neither as easy as Britain's nor as hard as the USA's — it is a mix of flexible and rigid.

blocks.title: The 24th Amendment Act (1971) — Parliament's reply to the Golaknath case (1967)
head: What it did
Meaning
rows: Declared that Parliament can reduce (abridge) or take away any Fundamental Right under Article 368
This undid the Golaknath case (1967), which had said Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights
A constitutional amendment is not a 'law' under Article 13, so Article 13 cannot be used to strike it down
The President must sign a duly passed amendment bill (cannot refuse or return it)
Changed the title of Article 368 (old title: 'Procedure for amendment of the Constitution') and added the words 'constituent power' and 'addition, variation or repeal' in Art 368(1)
Made it clear that Art 368 gives the power, not just the procedure
blocks.note: Clauses 368(4) and 368(5) were added later by the 42nd Amendment (1976), not by the 24th. Clause (4): no amendment can be questioned in any court. Clause (5): there is no limit on Parliament's power to amend.

blocks.text: see Basic structure doctrine — Golaknath, Kesavananda, Minerva Mills

blocks.title: How an amendment bill becomes law

steps.step: 1. Introduce the bill in either House of Parliament
steps.detail: Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha. Never in a State Legislature.
A minister or a private member (an MP who is not a minister). No prior permission or recommendation of the President is needed.

steps.step: 3. Pass it in each House by special majority
steps.detail: Two conditions together: (a) a majority of the total membership of the House, and (b) two-thirds of members present and voting.
If the two Houses disagree, there is NO joint sitting (joint sitting under Art 108 is only for ordinary bills).

steps.step: 5. Ratification by States (only for federal provisions)
steps.detail: Legislatures of at least half of the States must approve, by simple majority (majority of members present and voting). This comes BEFORE the President's assent.
The President must give assent. He or she cannot withhold assent or return the bill for reconsideration (24th Amendment, 1971).

steps.step: 7. It becomes a Constitutional Amendment Act
steps.detail: The Constitution now stands amended as the Act says.

blocks.title: Working out the numbers
head: Situation
Rule
Answer
rows: Majority of total membership = more than half of 400 = 201. Members present and voting = 390 − 30 = 360; two-thirds of 360 = 240. Both conditions must be met, so the bill needs the larger number.
State Assembly of 200; 160 present (other than Speaker); 40 abstain
Ratification needs only a simple majority of members present and voting. Voting = 160 − 40 = 120; more than half of 120 = 61
At least half must ratify: half of 29 = 14.5, so 15
blocks.note: 'Total membership' means all seats of the House, counting vacancies and absent members. Lok Sabha Rules apply the special majority at all effective stages of the bill, not only the final vote.

blocks.title: Other rules
items: Except for the special majority, an amendment bill is passed the same way as an ordinary bill.
A Money Bill route cannot be used: even if the subject is financial, each House must pass an amendment bill separately by special majority.
The Constitution fixes no time limit for States to ratify. Once half the States approve, it is enough — the other States need not act at all.

blocks.text: Article 368 itself provides only TWO types (special majority; special majority plus State ratification). A third type — simple majority — comes from other Articles and is not counted as an amendment 'for the purposes of Article 368'. So the Constitution can be changed in THREE ways.

head: Way
Majority needed
Examples
rows: Majority of members present and voting in each House, like an ordinary law
New States and State boundaries (Art 2, 3), citizenship (Art 11), Legislative Councils (Art 169), Fifth and Sixth Schedules
Majority of total membership AND two-thirds of present and voting, in each House
Fundamental Rights (Part III), Directive Principles (Part IV), and all provisions not in way 1 or way 3
3. Special majority plus ratification by half the States
The special majority of way 2, plus approval by a simple majority in the legislatures of at least half of the States
Federal provisions: election of the President, Seventh Schedule Lists, Supreme Court and High Courts, GST Council, Article 368 itself
Cannot be destroyed even by amendment

items: This is why the Indian Constitution is called partly rigid and partly flexible: some parts change by simple majority, others need a special majority and State consent.
A Fundamental Right or a Directive Principle does NOT need State ratification just because of its subject — it needs only the special majority.
Flexible constitution = amended by a simple (ordinary) procedure, as in Britain. Rigid constitution = needs a special procedure or special majority, as in the USA.

blocks.text: These are changed by an ordinary law of Parliament. The Articles below say so themselves, so Article 368 is not needed.

head: Matter
Article that allows ordinary law
rows: Admission or establishment of new States
Art 2. Art 4 says such a law is not an amendment under Art 368.
Forming new States; changing area, boundaries or names of States
Art 3. Art 4 says such a law is not an amendment under Art 368. The President must first refer the bill to the State Legislature concerned for its views.
Changes to the First and Fourth Schedules made by such laws
Creating or abolishing a State Legislative Council
Art 169. The State Assembly first passes a resolution by special majority. Parliament may then pass a law, but it is not bound to. Art 169(3) says such a law is not an amendment under Art 368.
Second Schedule — emoluments, allowances and privileges of the President, Governors, Speakers, judges etc.
The Article for each office (for example, Supreme Court judges' salaries by law under Art 125(1); a State Speaker's salary by the State Legislature under Art 186)
Art 118 (each House makes its own rules of procedure)
Privileges of Parliament, its members and committees
Art 105(3) (Art 194(3) for State Legislatures). Parliament may define privileges by ordinary law; it cannot rewrite the rest of Art 105 this way.
Use of English in Parliament after 15 years
Number of puisne judges (judges other than the Chief Justice) of the Supreme Court
Giving more jurisdiction to the Supreme Court
Art 138 (more jurisdiction); Art 139 (power to issue writs for purposes other than Art 32)
Use of official language (for example, continuing English for Union purposes)
Elections to Parliament and State Legislatures
Union Territories (for example, creating a legislature for Puducherry)
Art 239A. Art 239A(2) says such a law is not an amendment under Art 368, even if it changes the Constitution
Fifth Schedule — Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
Sixth Schedule — tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram
blocks.note: Trap: changing the TEXT of Art 124 itself is not ordinary law — it needs special majority plus ratification (Supreme Court is a federal provision).

sections.heading: Federal provisions — need ratification by half the States

blocks.title: Federal provisions in the proviso to Article 368(2)
head: Provision
Article / Part
rows: Election of the President and its manner
Extent of executive power of the Union and the States
Distribution of legislative powers between Union and States
Art 279A (added to the proviso by the 101st Amendment, 2016)
Any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule (Union, State, Concurrent)
Clause (d) of the proviso (seats of States in Rajya Sabha are listed in the Fourth Schedule)
Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution
blocks.note: NOT in this list: Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, emergency provisions, conditions of the Governor's office, the Preamble, abolition of Legislative Councils (Art 169, simple majority).

blocks.title: Examples to remember
head: Amendment / case
Point
rows: Needed ratification (it touches the Seventh Schedule and adds Art 279A). Assam was the first State to ratify it (12 August 2016).
Changed Fundamental Rights (Art 15, 16) only, so no State ratification was needed.

Para 7 of the Tenth Schedule (added by the 52nd Amendment, 1985) stopped the Supreme Court (Art 136) and High Courts (Art 226) from hearing disqualification cases. Because it changed the powers of courts, it needed State ratification but did not get it, so para 7 was struck down. It was severable (could be cut out), so the rest of the Tenth Schedule survived.
Union of India v Rajendra Shah (Supreme Court, 20 July 2021)

Part IX-B (Co-operative Societies, added by the 97th Amendment, 2011) was not ratified by the States. The Supreme Court held it valid only for multi-State co-operative societies. The 97th Amendment's other changes — adding 'co-operative societies' to Art 19(1)(c) and adding Art 43B — were not affected. (Gujarat High Court had struck it down in 2013.)

items: The role of States in the amendment process is limited: they cannot start an amendment and ratify only federal provisions.
Ratification by half the States is enough; it is not needed from all States, and not for every amendment.

head: Who / what
Why it cannot amend
rows: Cannot start an amendment bill. Only exception: it can pass a resolution asking Parliament to create or abolish its Legislative Council (Art 169) — Parliament may accept or ignore it.
Cannot start an amendment and cannot amend by ordinance. An ordinance (Art 123) acts like an ordinary Act, and an ordinary Act cannot amend the Constitution.
Not allowed for an amendment bill.
Referendum or a new Constituent Assembly
Not used in India. Parliament itself has the constituent power.
State law inserting itself into the Ninth Schedule
Not possible. Only Parliament, by a constitutional amendment, can add laws to the Ninth Schedule.
During an emergency, the federal system becomes unitary automatically by the Constitution's own provisions — no amendment is needed.

items: If Parliament dislikes a Supreme Court decision, it can pass a law to remove the basis of the decision, or pass a constitutional amendment to overcome it — but subject to the basic structure and judicial review.
Even an amendment passed with the full procedure (special majority and ratification) can be struck down by courts if it destroys the basic structure.

blocks.title: Criticism (Laxmikanth)
items: No special body like a Constitutional Convention (as in the USA) — Parliament itself amends.
States cannot start an amendment (unlike the USA).
Most of the Constitution can be amended by Parliament alone; only some provisions need States, and only half of them (USA needs three-fourths).
No time limit for States to ratify; silent on whether a State can withdraw its approval.
No joint sitting if the two Houses disagree, though ordinary bills have one.
The process is like ordinary law-making, except for the special majority.
The provisions are too sketchy, so many disputes go to the courts.

blocks.title: Who said what
head: Person
Said
rows: The procedure 'strikes a good balance between flexibility and rigidity'; and 'this variety in the amending process is wise but rarely found'
'There should be a certain flexibility. If you make any Constitution rigid and permanent, you stop the nation's growth'
The Assembly provided 'a facile (easy) procedure for amending the Constitution', unlike Canada, America or Australia

blocks.title: Comparison with other countries
head: Country
How amendment is approved
rows: Flexible: many changes can be made by an ordinary law

Proposed by two-thirds of both Houses of Congress (or by a convention called on the petition of two-thirds of States); ratified by three-fourths of States (38 of 50). The two-thirds vote only proposes; it does not complete ratification.
Referendum: a national majority of voters and majorities in a majority of the States
Mandatory referendum: majority of the people and of the Cantons
Special majority in Parliament, then ratification by at least half of the State legislatures

items: Either House can start an amendment — not only Lok Sabha. State Legislatures and the President cannot.
No prior permission or recommendation of the President is needed, even for a private member's bill.
No joint sitting for an amendment bill — each House passes it separately.
The President MUST give assent to an amendment bill (24th Amendment, 1971). A Money Bill also cannot be returned for reconsideration, but an ordinary bill can be returned once.
Ratification is needed only for federal provisions. Half (not all) of the States must approve, each by simple majority. It comes before the President's assent. There is no time limit.
Citizenship (Art 11), new States (Art 2, 3), Legislative Councils (Art 169), Fifth and Sixth Schedules are changed by simple majority, not under Art 368.
Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles need only a special majority. The Seventh Schedule Lists and Art 368 itself need a special majority plus ratification by half the States.
The 24th Amendment added Art 13(4) and Art 368(3); the 42nd Amendment added Art 368(4) and Art 368(5).

subcards.title: Major amendments
subcards.summary: Which amendment changed what, year by year, and the latest Bills.
at_a_glance: Right to Property removed from Fundamental Rights
44th Amendment Act, 1978 (now a legal right, Article 300A)
101st Amendment Act, 2016 (it was introduced as the 122nd Amendment Bill)
106th Amendment Act, 2023; in force from 16 April 2026, but seats are not yet actually reserved

blocks.title: How amendments are numbered
items: A Bill to amend the Constitution gets a Bill number when it is introduced. Only a Bill that becomes law gets an Amendment Act number.
So the two numbers usually differ. Example: the GST Bill was the 122nd Amendment Bill (2014); it became the 101st Amendment Act (2016).
Other examples: the EWS Bill was the 124th Bill and became the 103rd Act. The women's reservation Bill was the 128th Bill and became the 106th Act.
Many Bills never become law (they lapse or are defeated), so Bill numbers run ahead of Act numbers.

The year in an Act's title is usually the year Parliament passed it. The President's assent and the date it comes into force can be later. Examples: the 61st Act, 1988 got the President's assent and came into force on 28 March 1989; the 97th Act, 2011 came into force in 2012.
Total as of Nov 2026: 106 Amendment Acts. The 106th (2023) is the latest; no new Amendment Act was passed in 2024, 2025 or 2026 up to Nov 2026.

blocks.title: Bill number vs Act number (asked often)
head: Bill
Became
rows: Both passed by Lok Sabha but not passed by Rajya Sabha (the 65th was defeated there in October 1989); they lapsed. Later the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) did this.
None became law — see section on Bills of 2024–26

blocks.text: Note: Bills that only change a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe list (for example the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order (Amendment) Bill, 2021, which changed the SC list of Tamil Nadu) are ordinary laws that change a Presidential Order. They are not Constitutional Amendment Acts.
see Amendment procedure (Art 368) for how a Bill is passed

head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: First amendment ever, made by the Provisional Parliament under PM Jawaharlal Nehru (before the first Lok Sabha was elected). It: (1) inserted Article 15(4) — special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs; (2) inserted Articles 31A and 31B and added the Ninth Schedule, to save zamindari-abolition and land-reform laws from court challenge; (3) added three new grounds for restricting free speech in Article 19(2) — public order, friendly relations with foreign States, incitement to an offence — and made restrictions 'reasonable' (so courts can check them); (4) protected State trading and nationalisation from challenge under the right to trade.
Put the amount of compensation for property taken by the State beyond court review; extended Article 31A; added more Acts to the Ninth Schedule.
Added Entry 92A to the Union List — tax on inter-State sale of goods.

Reorganised States: ended the Part A, B, C, D classification and created 14 States and 6 Union Territories. Omitted old Parts VII and IX. Allowed one person to be Governor of two or more States (a proviso — an added exception — to Article 153). Allowed a common High Court for two or more States. Extended High Court jurisdiction to Union Territories. Provided for additional and acting High Court judges. Inserted Article 350B — a Special Officer for linguistic minorities. Also inserted Article 350A (mother-tongue teaching at primary stage).
Extended reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (SC/ST) and nomination of Anglo-Indians in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies up to 1970.
Allowed transfer of the Berubari Union (West Bengal) to Pakistan under the 1958 Indo-Pakistan Agreement.
Brought Dadra and Nagar Haveli into the Indian Union.
Vice-President to be elected by an electoral college (not a joint meeting of both Houses).
Brought Goa, Daman and Diu into the Indian Union.
Statehood to Nagaland with special provisions (Article 371A).
Brought Puducherry into the Union; allowed legislatures for some Union Territories (Article 239A).

Raised retirement age of High Court judges from 60 to 62. Let a High Court issue writs to authorities outside its territory if the cause of action (the facts that give the right to go to court) arose within its territory. Allowed a retired High Court judge to act as ad hoc (temporary) Supreme Court judge.
Allowed restrictions on speech, assembly and association in the interest of 'sovereignty and integrity of India'.
Land under personal cultivation (within the ceiling limit) can be taken only on paying market value (proviso to Article 31A). Added 44 more Acts to the Ninth Schedule.
Added Sindhi as the 15th language in the Eighth Schedule.
Extended SC/ST reservation and Anglo-Indian nomination to 1980.
blocks.note: 'Eminent domain' (the State's legal power to take private property for a public purpose) is the idea behind the property amendments of the 1950s, including the 4th (1955).

blocks.text: Why the 1st Amendment matters: it was made to overcome court judgments on fundamental rights (land reform and free speech cases of 1950–51). So it is called the first amendment made to get around judicial interpretation of Fundamental Rights.

head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Response to the Golak Nath case (1967). Inserted Article 13(4) and Article 368(3): Article 13 does not apply to a constitutional amendment. Said Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, 'by way of addition, variation or repeal'. This is called constituent power — the power to change the Constitution itself, different from ordinary law-making. Changed the heading of Article 368 to 'Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor'. Made the President's assent to an amendment Bill compulsory.

Cut down the right to property: in Article 31(2) the word 'amount' replaced 'compensation', and a law cannot be challenged just because the amount is paid fully or partly in a form other than cash. (Public purpose and authority of law were still needed.) Inserted Article 31C — a law giving effect to Article 39(b) or 39(c) cannot be challenged under Articles 14, 19 and 31.
Abolished privy purses (payments) and privileges of former princely rulers. Omitted Articles 291 and 362; inserted Article 363A; changed the definition of 'Ruler' in Article 366(22).

Raised the maximum number of Lok Sabha seats from 525 to 545: seats from States raised from 500 to 525; seats from Union Territories reduced from 25 to 20. (The Act's title year is 1973 — President's assent 17 October 1973; Laxmikanth's list shows it as 1972.)
Special provisions for Andhra Pradesh (Telangana region): Articles 371D and 371E.
Made Sikkim an 'associate State' (a new Tenth Schedule, later removed).
Made Sikkim a full State (Article 371F); removed that Tenth Schedule.
Made the declaration of emergency and ordinances non-justiciable (cannot be questioned in court).

Inserted Article 329A: election disputes of the President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Speaker were put beyond the courts. Clause (4) of Article 329A was struck down in the Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain case (1975). The 44th Amendment later omitted Article 329A.
Substituted Article 297: Parliament can fix the limits of territorial waters, continental shelf, exclusive economic zone and maritime zones. Added 64 laws to the Ninth Schedule.
Raised retirement age of State Public Service Commission members from 60 to 62.

Made by the Janata Government to undo parts of the 42nd. Restored the power of the Supreme Court and High Courts over judicial review and writs. Omitted Articles 131A and 226A (and 31D, 32A, 144A, 228A). Took away Parliament's special power to make laws against anti-national activities (Article 31D).

head: 42nd Amendment (1976) — called 'Mini-Constitution'
rows: Most comprehensive amendment so far; based on the Swaran Singh Committee. Introduced in Lok Sabha on 1 September 1976. Made under PM Indira Gandhi during the Emergency. It changed the Preamble, the Seventh Schedule and many Articles.
Added three words to the Preamble: Socialist, Secular, Integrity. (This is the only time the Preamble has been amended.)
Added Fundamental Duties — new Part IVA, Article 51A.
Made the President bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74(1)).
Added Part XIVA on Tribunals (Articles 323A administrative tribunals and 323B other tribunals).
Froze the number of seats in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies at the 1971 census level until 2001 (that is, until the figures of the first census after 2000 are published).
Inserted Article 368(4) and (5): no amendment can be questioned in court and Parliament's amending power has no limit. Struck down in the Minerva Mills case (1980).

Cut down the power of the Supreme Court and High Courts to do judicial review and issue writs. Example: Article 131A gave only the Supreme Court the power to decide whether a Central law is valid; Article 226A limited the High Courts. (Both were omitted by the 43rd.)
Raised the term of Lok Sabha and State Assemblies from 5 to 6 years.

Laws made to carry out ANY Directive Principle cannot be struck down for violating some Fundamental Rights — Article 31C was extended to all Directive Principles (earlier only Article 39(b) and 39(c)). This extension was struck down in the Minerva Mills case (1980).
Let Parliament make laws against anti-national activities that override Fundamental Rights (Article 31D, later omitted by the 43rd).

Added new Directive Principles: Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), Article 43A (workers' participation in management of industries), Article 48A (protection of environment, forests and wildlife). Also changed Article 39(f) (healthy development of children).
National emergency can be declared for a part of India.
President's rule in a State: the period allowed at one time raised from 6 months to 1 year.
Centre can deploy its armed forces in any State for a grave law-and-order situation (Entry 2A added to the Union List).

Moved five subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List: education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and administration of justice (organisation of courts other than the Supreme Court and High Courts).
Removed the quorum requirement in Parliament and State legislatures.
Allowed Parliament to decide, from time to time, the rights and privileges of its members and its committees.
Provided for an All-India Judicial Service.
Shortened the procedure for disciplinary action against civil servants: removed their right to make a representation at the second stage after the inquiry (that is, against the penalty proposed).
blocks.title: 42nd Amendment — full list

head: 44th Amendment (1978) — made by the Janata Government (PM Morarji Desai) to undo the 42nd
rows: Restored the term of Lok Sabha and State Assemblies to 5 years.
President can send the Cabinet's advice back once for reconsideration; the advice given after reconsideration binds the President.
'Armed rebellion' replaced 'internal disturbance' as a ground for national emergency (Article 352).
National emergency only on the written recommendation of the Cabinet.
Rights under Article 20 and Article 21 cannot be suspended during a national emergency.
Removed the Right to Property from Fundamental Rights: omitted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31. It is now a legal right under Article 300A (Part XII), inserted by this amendment.
Gave back to the courts the power to decide election disputes of the President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Speaker of Lok Sabha. (For the PM and Speaker this meant omitting Article 329A.)
Gave constitutional protection to newspaper reports of proceedings of Parliament and State legislatures (Article 361A).
Inserted Article 38(2) Directive Principle: the State shall reduce inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities.
Removed the rule that the satisfaction of the President or Governor in issuing ordinances is final (cannot be checked).
Added procedural safeguards for national emergency and President's rule.
Omitted the reference to the British House of Commons in the Articles on parliamentary privileges.
Restored some of the powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts (taken away by the 42nd).
blocks.title: 44th Amendment — full list
blocks.note: The 44th did NOT remove 'Socialist' and 'Secular' from the Preamble and did NOT omit Fundamental Duties.

head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Extended SC/ST reservation and Anglo-Indian nomination to 1990.
Sales tax changes; added Entry 92B to the Union List (tax on consignment of goods).
Anti-defection law: added the Tenth Schedule (disqualifying MPs and MLAs who defect). PM Rajiv Gandhi.
Goa Assembly to have at least 30 members (Article 371-I).
Inserted Article 394A: authoritative Hindi text of the Constitution, published under the authority of the President (not the Governor).
Raised the ceiling on profession tax from ₹250 to ₹2,500 a year (Article 276).
Reduced the voting age from 21 to 18 years by amending Article 326. PM Rajiv Gandhi. (President's assent and coming into force: 28 March 1989.)
Extended SC/ST reservation and Anglo-Indian nomination to 2000.
Created a multi-member National Commission for SCs and STs in place of the Special Officer (Article 338).
Made Delhi the National Capital Territory with a 70-member Assembly and 7-member Council of Ministers (Articles 239AA, 239AB).
Added elected members of the Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies to the electoral college for electing the President.
Added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali to the Eighth Schedule (total 18 languages).
Constitutional status to Panchayati Raj: Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects). In force 24 April 1993.
Constitutional status to Municipalities: Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects); includes Article 243ZD (District Planning Committee). In force 1 June 1993.
Rent tribunals at State level (amended Article 323B).
Put the Tamil Nadu reservation law (69% reservation) into the Ninth Schedule. (The Supreme Court in 1992 had capped reservation at 50%.)
Reservation in promotion for SCs and STs — inserted Article 16(4A).
Extended SC/ST reservation and Anglo-Indian nomination to 2010.

blocks.title: Stages of the SC/ST Commission (Article 338)
head: Year
Stage
rows: Special Officer (Commissioner for SCs and STs) under the original Article 338
Non-statutory Commission for SCs and STs set up by a government resolution
Renamed National Commission for SCs and STs (still non-statutory)
First constitutional multi-member National Commission for SCs and STs set up (after the 65th Amendment, 1990)
89th Amendment split it into two: Commission for SCs (Article 338) and Commission for STs (Article 338A)

blocks.text: Lok Sabha seats from States were raised by the 7th (1956) and the 31st (1973) Amendments.

head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: 'Alternative scheme of devolution' on the recommendation of the 10th Finance Commission: States get a share of all central taxes (not only income tax and Union excise duties). Omitted Article 272. The 29% share is NOT written in the Constitution.
Backlog (unfilled) reserved vacancies of a year are treated as a separate class; the 50% ceiling does not apply to them (Article 16(4B)).
Amended Article 335: allows relaxing qualifying marks or lowering evaluation standards for SCs and STs in promotion reservation in Central and State services.
No SC reservation needed in panchayats in Arunachal Pradesh (no SCs live there).
Extended the freeze on the number of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats until the first census after 2026. Allowed redrawing of constituency boundaries inside States on the 1991 census.
'Consequential seniority' for SC/ST government servants promoted under reservation: they keep the seniority that comes with the promotion. With effect from June 1995.

Inserted Article 21A: free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 is a Fundamental Right. Changed Article 45: early childhood care and education for children below 6. Added Fundamental Duty Article 51A(k): parents must give education opportunities to children aged 6–14.
Constituency boundaries inside States to be redrawn on the 2001 census (not 1991); also used 2001 census for SC/ST seat reservation (Articles 330, 332). It did NOT increase the number of seats.
Service tax: inserted Article 268A (later omitted by the 101st).
Separate National Commission for STs (Article 338A); the National Commission for SCs continues under Article 338.

Council of Ministers capped: Union — at most 15% of total Lok Sabha members, including the PM (Article 75(1A)); State — at most 15% of Assembly, including the CM, but not less than 12 (Article 164(1A)). Defectors cannot become ministers or hold paid political posts. Deleted the 'split' exception from the Tenth Schedule (earlier, if one-third of a party's members left together, it was called a 'split' and they were not disqualified).
Added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali to the Eighth Schedule (total 22 languages).

Inserted Article 15(5): reservation for backward classes, SCs and STs in admission to educational institutions, including private ones (aided or unaided), except minority institutions. Response to the P.A. Inamdar case (2005).
Tribal welfare minister: Bihar freed from this duty; it now applies to Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha (Article 164).
Extended SC/ST reservation and Anglo-Indian nomination to 2020.

Co-operative societies: added 'co-operative societies' to Article 19(1)(c) (a Fundamental Right); inserted Article 43B (a Directive Principle — not enforceable); added Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT).
Special provisions for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region (Article 371J).
Created the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) in place of the collegium. Struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015.

Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh (1974 agreement, 2011 Protocol): exchange of enclaves (small pieces of one country's land lying inside the other country); changed the First Schedule for Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya and Tripura. Assent: President Pranab Mukherjee.

GST: inserted Article 246A (both Parliament and State legislatures can make GST laws), Article 269A (inter-State GST) and Article 279A (GST Council). Omitted Article 268A. Needed ratification by half the States; Assam was the first State to ratify.
Constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes (Article 338B); inserted Article 342A.
EWS reservation: inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6) — up to 10% for economically weaker sections, in addition to existing reservation. It did NOT need ratification by States.
Extended SC/ST seat reservation in Lok Sabha and Assemblies to 80 years from the start of the Constitution (to January 2030). Ended Anglo-Indian nomination to Lok Sabha and Assemblies.
Restored the power of States to make their own list of socially and educationally backward classes (Article 342A(3)).

blocks.title: Extra details asked in exams

GST timeline, in order: 115th Bill (2011, lapsed); then 122nd Bill (2014); then President's assent to the 101st Act (8 September 2016); then the President's order setting up the GST Council (September 2016); then the first GST Council meeting (September 2016); then GST came into force on 1 July 2017.

The GST Council has been a constitutional body under Article 279A from the start; it was never a statutory body (one made by an ordinary law) first. It recommends the turnover limit below which goods and services may be exempted. GST is a destination-based indirect tax (the tax goes to the State where the goods or services are consumed).

subcards.title: Basic structure doctrine
subcards.summary: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but not its basic structure.

sections.heading: How the doctrine grew: Parliament vs Supreme Court

blocks.text: The question: can Parliament use Article 368 (the power to amend the Constitution) to cut down Fundamental Rights? Article 13(2) says the State shall not make any 'law' that takes away Fundamental Rights. So the fight was over one word: is a constitutional amendment a 'law' under Article 13?

items.detail: Challenge to the 1st Amendment (it cut the right to property). Held: Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights, because 'law' in Article 13 means only ordinary laws, not constitutional amendments. So the 1st Amendment was upheld.
Held that Directive Principles must give way to Fundamental Rights. It led to the 1st Amendment. (Not a basic-structure case, but comes first in chronology questions.)

Followed Shankari Prasad and upheld the 17th Amendment, holding that an amendment is not 'law' under Article 13. Justice Mudholkar, in a separate opinion, first asked whether the 'basic features' of the Constitution could be changed by amendment.

11 judges, 6:5. Reversed the earlier view. Fundamental Rights have a 'transcendental and immutable' (above change, fixed) position. An amendment IS 'law' under Article 13(2), so Parliament cannot take away or abridge (cut down) Fundamental Rights.

Parliament's reply to Golak Nath. Inserted Article 13(4) and Article 368(3): Article 13 does not apply to amendments made under Article 368. Parliament can amend any part, including Fundamental Rights, by addition, variation or repeal.
13 judges, 7:6. Overruled Golak Nath. Upheld the 24th Amendment. But laid down the 'basic structure' doctrine: Parliament can amend any part, but cannot alter the basic structure.

items.what: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain case (1975)
items.detail: Reaffirmed and applied the doctrine. Struck down clause (4) of Article 329A (39th Amendment), which kept disputes about the election of the Prime Minister and the Lok Sabha Speaker outside the reach of all courts.
Parliament's reply. Added clauses (4) and (5) to Article 368. Clause (4): no amendment can be questioned in any court. Clause (5): there is no limit on Parliament's power to amend.
Struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368. Held that the limited nature of the amending power, and judicial review (the courts' power to check laws), are themselves basic features.
Held that the basic structure test applies to amendments made after 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda judgment).
Later cases that used it: S.R. Bommai (1994), L. Chandra Kumar (1997), I.R. Coelho (2007), NJAC case (2015) and Janhit Abhiyan (2022).

blocks.title: Present position (Laxmikanth)
items: Parliament under Article 368 can amend ANY part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but WITHOUT affecting the basic structure.
The words 'basic structure' are NOT written anywhere in the Constitution (not in Article 368, not in the original 1950 text). It is a judge-made doctrine.
The Supreme Court has never given one final list of basic features. Courts identify them case by case.
So even an amendment passed with the correct special majority and state ratification can be struck down if it damages the basic structure.

Bench of 11 judges, 6:5. Parliament cannot abridge Fundamental Rights. Amendment is 'law' under Article 13(2).
Used 'prospective overruling' (new rule applies only to the future), so the 1st (1951), 4th (1955) and 17th (1964) Amendments stayed valid. They were NOT declared void.
Decided 24 April 1973. 13 judges (largest bench ever), 7:6. Chief Justice S.M. Sikri presided. Overruled Golak Nath. Upheld the 24th Amendment.

Struck down Article 329A(4) of the 39th Amendment.
First case where the doctrine was APPLIED to strike down an amendment clause. Free and fair elections and judicial review are basic features. Also called the 'Election case'.

Three basic features: the limited power to amend, judicial review, and the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

Also called the 'Ninth Schedule case'. Judicial review cannot be removed by putting a law in the Ninth Schedule.

5 judges, 4:1. Struck down the 99th Amendment (2014) and the NJAC Act (2014) – both void.
Independence of the judiciary is a basic feature. The collegium system (senior judges choosing judges) came back. Only Justice J. Chelameswar dissented (disagreed): he would have upheld the NJAC.

blocks.title: Prospective overruling (used in Golak Nath)
head: Aspect
Meaning
rows: Court overrules an old ruling but applies the new rule only to the FUTURE. Past actions stay valid.
It comes from American law. It was first used in India in the Golak Nath case (1967).
From 1967, Parliament could not abridge Fundamental Rights. But earlier amendments (1st, 4th, 17th) were not struck down.

sections.heading: Amendments in the fight (and what courts did)

head: Amendment (year)
Change
What the Supreme Court did
rows: Added Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule.
Added more state land laws to the Ninth Schedule.
Upheld in Sajjan Singh; left valid in Golak Nath.

Reply to Golak Nath. Inserted Article 13(4) and Article 368(3): Article 13 does not apply to amendments. Parliament can amend any part, including Fundamental Rights, by addition, variation or repeal. President MUST give assent to an amendment bill.

Inserted Article 31C in two parts. First part: laws made to carry out Article 39(b) and 39(c) cannot be challenged for violating Article 14 or Article 19. Second part: if a law declares that it gives effect to this policy, no court can question that declaration.
In Kesavananda Bharati, the first part was held valid. The second part (no court review) was struck down, because judicial review is a basic feature.
Inserted Article 329A: disputes about the election of the Prime Minister and the Lok Sabha Speaker were kept out of all courts.
Clause (4) struck down in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975). Article 329A was later omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978).

Did three things here. (1) Added clauses (4) and (5) to Article 368: no court can question an amendment, and there is no limit on the amending power. (2) Widened Article 31C to cover ALL Directive Principles. (3) Added Article 226A, which stopped High Courts from testing the validity of Central laws.
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 and the widening of Article 31C. Only those parts were struck down – not the whole 42nd Amendment.
Omitted Article 226A, restoring High Court power to test Central laws.

blocks.title: Today
items: Article 31C now protects only laws made for Article 39(b) and 39(c), and only against challenge under Article 14 and Article 19. It does NOT cover every Directive Principle.
A High Court under Article 226 can also examine whether a constitutional amendment is valid.
Article 31 (right to property) was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978).

Ideas created by judges (not written in the Constitution): Public Interest Litigation (PIL), the basic structure, and limits on handcuffing prisoners. But the exceptions (limits) to Fundamental Rights are written in Part III itself – they were NOT made by courts.

If Parliament does not like a Supreme Court decision, it can pass a new law or a constitutional amendment to get around it (for example, the 24th Amendment after Golak Nath). But the amendment must still respect the basic structure.

blocks.title: NOT basic features
items: Judicial activism is NOT a basic feature (judicial review is).
Right to property is not a basic feature. It is now only a legal right (not a Fundamental Right) under Article 300A.
'Federalism is basic' does NOT mean state boundaries can never change – Article 3 still allows it.
A provision linked to a basic feature can still be amended. The test is whether the amendment DAMAGES that feature.

items: Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule were added by the 1st Amendment (1951). Laws put in the Ninth Schedule are protected from being challenged for violating Fundamental Rights.
Only Parliament can put a law in the Ninth Schedule, and it must do so by a constitutional amendment.
It had 13 Acts originally; it now has 282 (as per Laxmikanth).

items: No 'blanket immunity' (complete protection) from judicial review for Ninth Schedule laws.

head: Case (year)
Held
rows: Preamble is NOT part of the Constitution (but helps interpret it).
Rejected Berubari. Preamble IS part of the Constitution. It CAN be amended under Article 368, but its basic features cannot be altered.
Secularism is a basic feature (held by a 9-judge bench).
Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution (same as Kesavananda).

items: The Preamble does not give any power to the legislature, does not limit its power, and cannot be enforced in courts.
The word 'Secular' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976). But secularism was held to be a basic feature because of the Constitution as a whole – not because of that one word.
Was it in the original (1950) Constitution? Union Public Service Commission – YES. The word 'Secular', Fundamental Duties and the basic structure – NO.
The basic structure doctrine was FIRST laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) – not in Golak Nath, and not in the Indira Gandhi case (1975). The Indira Gandhi case was the first to APPLY it.
Bench sizes: Kesavananda Bharati – 13 judges, 7:6, 24 April 1973, Chief Justice S.M. Sikri presiding. Golak Nath – 11 judges, 6:5. I.R. Coelho – 9 judges. NJAC case – 5 judges, 4:1.
Who replied to whom: the 24th Amendment (1971) replied to Golak Nath. The 42nd Amendment (1976) replied to Kesavananda and the Indira Gandhi case. Minerva Mills (1980) replied to the 42nd Amendment.
Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 were added by the 42nd Amendment (not the 44th) and struck down in Minerva Mills.
Article 329A was inserted by the 39th Amendment and omitted by the 44th.
Ninth Schedule laws are NOT fully protected. Those added after 24 April 1973 can be tested against the basic structure.
The Constitution does NOT define 'basic structure' or 'judicial review'. Both terms come from court judgments.

Judicial review is a basic feature; judicial activism (courts actively making policy) is not. The doctrine does not make courts supreme over Parliament, or Parliament over courts – the Constitution is supreme. (Note: one previous exam question gives the answer as 'in accord with procedure established by law'.)
